title: The risk register
blurb: What a risk register records, field by field, and the six jobs it does for a project.
question: A sponsor asks the project manager for one document showing every current threat and opportunity, how likely and serious each is, who owns it and what is being done about it. What should the project manager hand over, and why is it trusted?

teach.h: One living record of every risk
teach.body: A risk register is the log that records the project's identified risks and how each one is being managed. In plain English: it is the single, shared list of 'what could happen, how much it matters, who is on it and what we are doing about it'. It holds threats AND opportunities, and it is a living document: opened when the first risk is identified and kept up to date until the last risk is closed.

teach.caption: R03 is an opportunity: registers hold both. A full register also records cause, event and effect, proximity, actions, status and residual risk.

teach.h: The fields of a register entry
teach.caption: Grouping the fields by what you do with them makes the list easy to recall.

teach.body: Every risk gets a named RISK OWNER: the person accountable for managing that risk and making sure its response works. The individual tasks within a response can be given to ACTION OWNERS, who carry them out and report back. On the library job the site lead owns R01; the surveyor who books the asbestos survey is an action owner. Clear names in the register mean nothing is left to 'somebody'.

teach.h: Six uses of a risk register
items: Central record: one place holding every identified risk.
Prioritisation: scores show which risks deserve attention first.
Ownership: a named owner for every risk, so accountability is clear.
Tracking: responses, actions and status are followed through to closure.
Communication and reporting: one shared picture for team, sponsor and board.
Audit trail: a history of what was decided, by whom and when.

teach.h: One entry over time: R01 asbestos
teach.caption: Each review updates the same entry: scores, status and residual risk change as the response works.

teach.body: A register written at the start and never reopened is worthless. Risks change: new ones appear, scores rise and fall as responses work, and some pass or occur. The project manager reviews the register regularly, often at every progress meeting, updating scores, status and residual risk, and closing entries that no longer apply. Kept current, it lets the team and sponsor make decisions on today's facts, not last month's.

teach.caption: When a threat on the register actually occurs, its entry is closed and, if it breaches tolerances, it is raised as an issue.

teach.h: Would you find it in a risk register?
teach.note: Actual progress belongs in progress reports; payments belong in financial controls.

teach.text: The register is a RECORD, not the process. It does not find risks for you and it does not assess them: people do that in workshops and analysis, then write the results in the register. If an option describes 'a structured way to identify risks' or 'a method for assessing likelihood', it is describing the risk process, not the register.

items: Risk register: the record of identified risks (threats and opportunities) and how each is managed.
Key fields: ID, description, category, owner, probability, impact, score, proximity, response, actions, status, residual risk, dates.
Uses: central record, prioritisation, ownership, tracking, communication and reporting, audit trail.
It is a living document, reviewed and updated throughout the project.

summary: You can now describe what a risk register is, list the fields it holds and explain its six uses. You can also tell it apart from the risk process itself and from the issue log.

A.q: Which of the following best describes a risk register?
options: A record of risks and how each is managed
A process for finding risks in workshops
A chart plotting probability by impact
A log of problems that have now occurred
A.why: A risk register records the identified risks and how each one is being managed: owner, scores, response, actions and status.

whyNot.1: Workshops are part of the identification process; the register only records what they find.
whyNot.2: A probability-impact chart is an analysis tool. Scores are written into the register, but the chart is not the register.
whyNot.3: Problems that have occurred are issues, recorded in the issue log.

A.q: In a risk register, what does the 'residual risk' field record?
options: The risk score before any response is chosen
The risks that were closed at the last review
The risk that remains after the response
The contingency held for all of the risks
A.why: Residual risk is the exposure left once the planned response has been applied, so the team can see whether it is now acceptable.

whyNot.0: The score before any response is the original assessment, not the residual risk.
whyNot.1: Closed risks are shown by their status, not by a residual risk figure.
whyNot.3: Contingency is a reserve of time or money; it is not what residual risk measures.

A.q: Which risk register field makes one person accountable for managing each risk?
options: Proximity
Category
Impact score
Risk owner
A.why: The risk owner is the named person accountable for managing the risk and making sure its response is carried out.

whyNot.0: Proximity records how soon the risk could occur.
whyNot.1: Category groups risks by type or source, such as technical or commercial.
whyNot.2: The impact score rates how serious the effect would be, not who is responsible.

B.q:
Which TWO of the following are uses of a risk register?
1. Providing an audit trail of risk decisions.
2. Approving changes to the project baseline.
3. Showing which risks should be prioritised.
4. Replacing the need for risk workshops.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: The register keeps a history of decisions (audit trail) and its scores show which risks to deal with first (prioritisation).

whyNot.0: Approving baseline changes is the job of change control, not the risk register.
whyNot.2: Neither is a use: baseline changes go through change control, and the register records what workshops find rather than replacing them.
whyNot.3: Prioritisation is a use, but the register does not replace workshops: risks still have to be identified by people.

B.q: What does the 'proximity' field in a risk register show?
options: How soon the risk could occur
How close the risk is to closure
How near the score is to red
How many people the risk affects
B.why: Proximity records when the risk could happen, helping the team decide which risks need action soonest.

whyNot.1: How near a risk is to being closed is shown by its status, not its proximity.
whyNot.2: The colour band comes from the probability and impact score.
whyNot.3: The reach of a risk is part of its impact description, not its proximity.

B.q: Which of the following would NOT normally be recorded in a risk register?
options: The planned response to each risk
The current status of each risk
The invoices paid to each supplier
The impact score for each risk
B.why: Supplier invoices are financial records handled by financial controls. They have no place in a risk register.

whyNot.0: The planned response is a core field: it shows how each risk will be treated.
whyNot.1: Status (open, closed, occurred) is tracked against every entry.
whyNot.3: Impact, with probability, is how each risk is scored and prioritised.

C.q: On the Riverside Library project, a survey shows asbestos (R01) is far less likely than first feared. What should the project manager do with entry R01?
options: Delete it, as the threat has now gone away
Update its scores, status and residual risk
Move it into the issue log for the sponsor
Leave it unchanged until project closure
C.why: The register is a living document: the entry is updated to show the new assessment, keeping the record current and the audit trail intact.

whyNot.0: Deleting entries destroys the audit trail. Risks are closed and kept, never simply removed.
whyNot.2: Nothing has happened that breaches tolerance, so it is not an issue.
whyNot.3: Leaving out-of-date scores means decisions are made on old information.

C.q: A sponsor wants to see, in one place, the project's current threats and opportunities, who owns each and what is being done about them. What should the project manager show?
options: The issue log
The change log
The project schedule
The risk register
C.why: The risk register holds every identified risk with its owner, scores and response, giving the sponsor a single, current picture.

whyNot.0: The issue log records problems that have already occurred, not possible future events.
whyNot.1: The change log records requests to change the baseline and their decisions.
whyNot.2: The schedule shows activities and dates, not risks and their responses.

C.q: Why is a risk register described as a 'living document'?
options: It is drafted at initiation and then archived
It may be edited by any stakeholder at any time
It is reviewed and updated throughout the project
It replaces the project plan once work has begun
C.why: Risks change constantly, so the register is reviewed and updated regularly from start to finish.

whyNot.0: A register that is written once and archived goes out of date immediately.
whyNot.1: 'Living' means kept current, not open to uncontrolled edits; entries have owners.
whyNot.3: The register supports the plan; it never replaces it.

reteach.title: The wedding 'what-if' list
reteach.question: A couple planning a wedding keep a list on the fridge of everything that might go wrong (or right) on the day. How is that list just like a risk register?

blocks.body: For each 'what if', the couple note how likely it is, how much it would matter, who is dealing with it and the plan. Every week they update it: the marquee is booked, so rain matters less; the caterer has confirmed, so that line is closed. That is a risk register: a record of risks, owners and responses, kept current until the big day.

blocks.caption: The sunny evening is an opportunity: a register holds the good 'what ifs' too.

items: Each line: the risk, how likely and serious, an owner and a plan.
Updated every week, so it always shows today's picture.
It records the plan; it doesn't make the plan for you.

explain.body: Each entry starts with an ID and a clear description, ideally written as cause, event and effect. It is then assessed: a probability (how likely) and an impact (how serious) combine into a score that sets its priority, and proximity shows how soon it could happen.

head: Field
Answers the question
rows: How bad (or good) would it be?

test.q: Which risk register field records how likely a risk is to occur?
options: Impact
Probability
Proximity
Category
test.why: Probability (likelihood) records the chance of the risk occurring.

whyNot.0: Impact records how serious the effect would be.
whyNot.2: Proximity records how soon it could occur.
whyNot.3: Category records the type or source of the risk.

explain.body: The response type (for example reduce or enhance) and its actions are recorded with a risk owner, accountable for the risk, and action owners, who carry out specific tasks. Status, review dates and residual risk show how things stand now.

test.q: What is the difference between a risk owner and an action owner?
options: Risk owners are accountable; action owners do tasks
Risk owners score risks; action owners approve them
Risk owners are sponsors; action owners are users
Risk owners close risks; action owners identify them
test.why: The risk owner is accountable for managing the risk overall; action owners carry out specific actions within the response.

whyNot.1: Scoring is part of analysis, and action owners don't approve risks.
whyNot.2: Risk owners can be anyone best placed to manage the risk, not only sponsors.
whyNot.3: Identification is done by the whole team, not by action owners.

explain.body: Six uses: a central record, prioritisation, clear ownership, tracking responses to closure, communicating and reporting risk to the team, sponsor and board, and an audit trail of decisions.

test.q: Which of the following is NOT a use of a risk register?
options: Communicating risk to the board
Prioritising which risks to treat
Recording who owns each risk
Deciding on change requests
test.why: Change requests are decided through change control. The register may inform the decision, but it isn't how the decision is made.

whyNot.0: Reporting and communicating risk is a core use.
whyNot.1: Scores in the register drive prioritisation.
whyNot.2: Clear ownership is one of its main purposes.

explain.body: The register is reviewed regularly. New risks are added, scores and status are updated as responses work, and risks that have passed or occurred are closed, never deleted, with lessons noted. That history is the audit trail.

test.q: A risk on the register has passed without occurring. What should happen to its entry?
options: Mark it closed and note any lessons
Delete it to keep the register short
Transfer it into the issue log
Raise its probability for next time
test.why: Risks that have passed are closed, keeping the record for the audit trail and capturing any lessons.

whyNot.1: Deleting entries loses the audit trail.
whyNot.2: Nothing has happened, so there is no issue to log.
whyNot.3: A passed risk can no longer occur on this project, so its probability isn't raised.
